Surah Saba' is Meccan, though it is said that the exception is His saying ﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ to the end of the verse. Its verses number fifty-four.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise belongs to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation and bounty. So to Him belongs praise in this world, for the perfection of His power and the completeness of His favour. ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾, because what is in the Hereafter is likewise. This is not the conjunction of the restricted with the unrestricted, for the description by which He is shown to be the Bestower of worldly bounties restricted the praise to them. The fronting of the relative clause (al-sila) indicates exclusivity (li'l-ikhtisas), for worldly bounties may come through the agency of one who deserves praise on their account, whereas this is not so with the bounties of the Hereafter. ﴿And He is the All-Wise﴾, who has perfected the affairs of both abodes. ﴿the All-Aware﴾ of the inner realities of things.

﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, such as rain that penetrates one place and springs forth in another, and treasures, hidden deposits, and the dead. ﴿And what comes forth from it﴾, such as living creatures, plants, metals, and the water of springs. ﴿And what descends from the heaven﴾, such as angels, books, decrees, provisions, dew, and thunderbolts. ﴿And what ascends into it﴾, such as angels, the deeds of servants, vapours, and smokes. ﴿And He is the Most Merciful, the All-Forgiving﴾ toward those who fall short in thanking Him for His bounties despite their abundance, or in the Hereafter, together with what He has of the earlier precedence of these lost bounties, by way of restriction (li'l-hasr).

**﴿And those who disbelieve say, "The Hour will not come upon us."﴾** This is a denial of its coming, or a mocking impatience at the promise of it.

**﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it will surely come upon you, the Knower of the unseen."﴾** This is a rejection of their statement and an affirmation of what they denied. It repeats the affirmation of its coming, emphasized by an oath (*qasam*), and describes the One sworn by with attributes that establish its possibility and negate the deeming of it unlikely, as has passed more than once.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read **﴿ʿAllāmi al-ghayb﴾** ("the Great Knower of the unseen") for intensification (*mubālagha*, emphasis by intensive form). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ruways read **﴿ʿĀlimi al-ghayb﴾** in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject or as the subject whose predicate is what follows.

**﴿Not an atom's weight in the heavens or in the earth escapes Him.﴾** Al-Kisa'i read **﴿yaʿzib﴾** with a kasra (*yaʿzibu*, the vowel of the verb's second radical). **﴿Nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear Record.﴾** This clause emphasizes the negation of escaping. The two words (*wa-lā aṣghara* and *wa-lā akbara*) are nominative, being subjects of an inchoative clause (*mubtada'*). The reading with a fatha, which makes them absolute negation of the genus (*nafy al-jins*), supports this. It is not permissible to take the nominative as coordinated with *mithqāl* and the fatha-ended forms as coordinated with *dharra*, on the grounds that the latter is in the genitive position but is given a fatha because of the diptotic form, since the exception (*istithnā'*) prevents this. The exception is possible only if the pronoun in *ʿanhu* refers to the unseen (*al-ghayb*), and what is recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh*) is taken as outside of it, because it is manifest to those who look at it. The meaning then is: nothing separates from the unseen except that it is written in the Tablet.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 4–5:

﴿That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ This is a cause (ʿillah) for His saying ﴿You will surely come to Me﴾, and an explanation of what necessitates its coming about. ﴿Those, for them is forgiveness and a generous provision﴾ — without toil in it, and without any reproach (mann) attached to it.

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by invalidating them and making people averse to them. ﴿Seeking to frustrate [Us]﴾ — competing, so that they might escape Us. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr recited (muʿajjizīn), meaning discouraging from faith whoever desires it. ﴿For them is a punishment of a painful kind (rijz)﴾ — of the evil kind of punishment. ﴿Painful (alim)﴾ — causing pain. Ibn Kathir, Yaʿqub and Hafs read it in the nominative (alimun).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 6:

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ (wa-yaʿlamu ulu al-ʿilm), meaning: those possessing knowledge among the Companions and those who followed them from the Community, or among the Muslims of the People of the Book. ﴿that what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ is the Qur'an. ﴿is the truth﴾ (huwa al-haqq). Whoever reads (al-haqqu) with a raised vowel makes huwa the subject (mubtada') and (al-haqqu) its predicate, and the clause is the second object of (yara) (ra'a). It is in the nominative and is a resumptive (mustaʾnaf) clause, serving to cite those possessing knowledge against the ignorant who strive against the signs. It has also been said that it is in the accusative, coordinated with (liyajziya) (so that He may recompense), meaning: and that those possessing knowledge may know, at the coming of the Hour, that it is the truth by direct witness, just as they know it now by proof. ﴿And He guides to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾, which is monotheism and clothing oneself in the garment of piety.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 34, verses 7–8:**

﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ And those who disbelieved said. Some of them said to others: ﴿هَلْ نَدُلُّكم عَلى رَجُلٍ﴾ "Shall we direct you to a man", meaning Muhammad, peace be upon him (ﷺ).

﴿يُنَبِّئُكُمْ﴾ "who will tell you," i.e., will inform you of the most wondrous of wonders. ﴿إذا مُزِّقْتُمْ كُلَّ مُمَزَّقٍ إنَّكم لَفي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾ "When you are torn to pieces utterly, indeed you will be in a new creation." That is, you will be brought into being as a new creation after your bodies have been torn apart in every manner of tearing and scattering, to the point that they become dust. The placement of the adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*, a temporal or locative complement) before its object indicates distance and emphasis on it. Its governing verb (*'āmil*) is omitted, and what follows indicates it, since what precedes it is not connected to it, and what follows it is its complement (*muḍāf ilayhi*). Alternatively, a barrier lies between it and its governing element. The word ﴿مُمَزَّقٍ﴾ (*mumazzaq*) may be a place noun, with the meaning: when you are torn apart and the floods carry you away in every direction and you are cast into every place. The word ﴿جَدِيدٍ﴾ (*jadīd*) is in the sense of an active participle from *jadda*, like ﴿حَدِيدٍ﴾ (*ḥadīd*) from *ḥadda*. It is said that it may also mean a passive participle from *jadda*, as when the weaver (*al-nassāj*) cuts the cloth.

﴿أفْتَرى عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا أمْ بِهِ جِنَّةٌ﴾ "Has he invented a lie against God, or is there madness in him?" *Jinnah* is madness, which gives him such illusions and places them upon his tongue. Their treatment of it as the counterpart (*qasīm*) of fabrication, while they did not believe in its truth, has been cited as evidence that between truth and falsehood there is an intermediate category, namely every report not based on insight into what is reported. Its weakness is evident, because fabrication (*iftirā'*) is more specific than falsehood (*kadhib*).

﴿بَلِ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ في العَذابِ والضَّلالِ البَعِيدِ﴾ "Rather, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error." This is God's rejection of their division, and an affirmation for them of something more terrible than both alternatives, namely the far-off error, far from the right course, such that deliverance from it is not hoped for, and the punishment that is its consequence. He placed it as a follow-up (*rasīl*, a consequence) to the error in occurrence and gave it precedence in wording to emphasize their deserving of it. The word ﴿البَعِيدِ﴾ (*al-ba'īd*, "far-off") is in origin an attribute of the one who errs, but it is ascribed to error (*al-ḍalāl*) by way of metaphorical attribution (*al-isnād al-majāzī*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 9:

﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and behind them of the heaven and the earth? If We wish, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them.﴾ This is a reminder of what they witness, which points to the perfect power of God, and which admits of removing their deeming the resurrection impossible, to the point that they made it a fabrication and a mockery; and it is also a threat. The meaning is: Are they blind, that they do not look at what encompasses them from every side, of heaven and earth, and do not reflect on whether they are harder to create, or the heaven? And [it is as if We said]: If We wish, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them, on account of their denial of the signs after the clear proofs have appeared. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (yasha') and (yakhsif) and (yusqit) with the letter ya' [as third-person verbs], in keeping with His saying: ﴿Has he invented a lie against God?﴾ Al-Kisa'i alone assimilates the fa' into the ba' [reading (yuskit bihim)], and Hafs reads (kisafan) with a vowel on the sin (kisafan, i.e., kisaf as a plural with fatha, from the vocalization of the sin). ﴿Indeed in that﴾ — the looking and reflecting upon these two — ﴿is surely a sign﴾ — a proof — ﴿for every servant who turns back in repentance﴾ — who returns to his Lord, for he is one who reflects much upon his affair.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 34, verses 10–11:**

﴿And We certainly gave David grace from Us.﴾ That is, over all the prophets, which is what is mentioned next. Or it means over all people, so that it includes prophethood, the Book, kingship, and a beautiful voice. ﴿O mountains, echo [his praises] with him!﴾ Repeat the glorification (tasbih) with him, or the lamentation over sin. This may happen either by creating a voice in the mountains like his voice, or by making them capable of glorifying God when they reflect on what is in them. Or it means: travel with him wherever he travels. It is also read as *awwibi*, from *al-awb* (returning), meaning: return to the glorification whenever he returns to it. This word is in apposition (*badal*) to *fadlan* or to *ataina*, with the verb "We said" or "We say" implied. ﴿And the birds.﴾ This is conjoined to the position (*mahall*) of "the mountains." The reading in the nominative (*raf*'), conjoining it to the word's own form, supports this, treating the built vowel that occurs here as if it were an inflectional vowel (*harakah i'rabiyya*). Alternatively, it is conjoined to *fadlan*, or it is an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul ma'ahu*) for *awwibi*. On this view, the nominative reading may also be by conjunction with the pronoun in *ma'ahu*. The original sentence would have been: "And We certainly gave David grace from Us: the echoing of the mountains and the birds." He changed this arrangement because of its grandeur and its indication of the great importance of his position and the majesty of his dominion, since He made the mountains and birds like rational beings submitting to his command, in the execution of his will over them. ﴿And We made iron soft for him.﴾ We made it in his hand like wax, which he shapes however he wishes, without heating it or hammering it with tools, or by his own strength.

﴿Make full coats of mail,﴾ We commanded him: "Make full coats of mail." Here *an* is either explanatory (*mufassira*) or verbal (*masdariyya*). ﴿Sabighat﴾ means wide coats of mail. It is also read as *sabighat*, and he was the first to make them. ﴿And measure well in the links,﴾ and measure well in their weaving, so that their rings are proportionate; or measure their nails, so that you do not make them thin and brittle, nor thick so that they tear.

It was reported that his coats of mail were not riveted, and this is supported by His saying: ﴿And We made iron soft for him.﴾

﴿Work righteousness,﴾ the pronoun in it refers to David and his family. ﴿Indeed, I am Seeing of what you do,﴾ so I will reward you for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 12–13:

﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind⁠—its morning [journey] was a month's [travel] and its evening [journey] was a month's [travel]⁠—﴾ That is, "We subjected the wind to him." It is also read "al-rīḥu" (in the nominative), meaning "and for Solomon the wind is subjected," and it is read "al-riyāḥu" (the winds). ﴿Its morning [journey] was a month's [travel], and its evening [journey] was a month's [travel].﴾ Its running in the morning covered the distance of a month's travel, and in the evening likewise. It is also read "ghudwatuhā" and "rawḥatuhā." ﴿And We caused a spring of molten brass to flow for him.﴾ The brass (al-qiṭr) was melted; He caused it to flow for him from its ore, so it gushed out of it like water gushing from a spring (yanbūʿ), and for this reason He called it a "spring" (ʿayn). This was in Yemen. ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him﴾: "and among the jinn" is coordinated with "the wind" (al-rīḥa), or it is a preposed circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a nominal sentence (mubtadaʾ and khabar). ﴿By the permission of his Lord﴾: by His command. ﴿And whoever of them deviates﴾: whoever of them turns away ﴿from Our command﴾: from what We commanded him of obedience to Solomon. It is also read "yazugh," from azāghahu. ﴿We will make him taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾: the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿They made for him whatever he willed of sanctuaries (maḥārīb)﴾: strong palaces and noble dwellings, named so because one defends them and fights over them. ﴿And statues (tamāthīl)﴾ and images, which were likenesses of angels and prophets according to the acts of worship they were accustomed to, so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. The prohibition of images is a renewed legislation (shar‘ mujaddad).

It is narrated that they made for him two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles above it. When he wished to ascend, the two lions spread their forelegs for him, and when he sat, the two eagles shaded him with their wings.

﴿And bowls (jifān)﴾ and platters. ﴿Like cisterns (al-jawāb)﴾: like large reservoirs, the plural of jābiyah, from al-jibāyah (collection), and it is one of the predominantly used descriptive nouns, like "ad-dābbah." ﴿And cauldrons fixed firmly﴾: fixed in their places upon the stones (al-athāfī), not moved from them because of their size. ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude (shukran)﴾: a quotation of what was said to them. "Shukran" is in the accusative, expressing purpose (ʿillah): "work for Him and worship Him in gratitude," or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), since the work for Him is gratitude, or a descriptive accusative, or a circumstantial accusative, or an object. ﴿And few of My servants are truly grateful (ash-shakūr)﴾: the one who devotes himself to rendering thanks with his heart, tongue and limbs for most of his time, and even with that his due is not fully rendered, because his being granted the ability to give thanks is a blessing that calls for another thanks, and so on without end. For this reason it was said: "The grateful one is he who sees his inability to give thanks."

﴿And bowls (jifān)﴾ and platters. ﴿Like cisterns (al-jawāb)﴾: like large reservoirs, the plural of jābiyah, from al-jibāyah (collection), and it is one of the predominantly used descriptive nouns, like "ad-dābbah." ﴿And cauldrons fixed firmly﴾: fixed in their places upon the stones (al-athāfī), not moved from them because of their size. ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude (shukran)﴾: a quotation of what was said to them. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 14–15:

﴿So when We decreed death upon him﴾, i.e., upon Sulayman. ﴿Nothing indicated to them his death﴾, i.e., nothing informed the jinn of it; and it is said, his family. ﴿Except a creature of the earth﴾, i.e., the termite (al-arada), which is ascribed to its action; it is also read with a fatha on the ra' (arada), and it means the wearing away of the wood by its action. It is said: the termite wore away the wood (artadat al-aradatu al-khashaba aradan), so it wore away (fa-artadat aradan), like the molars (al-qawadih) ate the teeth, eating (aklan), so it ate (fa-akalat aklan). ﴿Eating away at his staff﴾, his mina'ah (staff), from nasa'a al-ba'ir (nasa'a al-ba'ira), when he drove it, because it is driven with it. It is also read with a fatha on the mim and a lightened hamza, by substitution and deletion, contrary to analogy, since the analogy is to pronounce it between between (bayna bayn). "Minsa'atahu" is on the pattern mif'alah, like miydha'ah in maydha'ah. "Min sa'atihi", i.e., the tip of his staff, is a metaphor borrowed from sa'at al-qaws (the tip of the bow), and there are two dialects for it, as in qihah and quhah. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read minsa'atahu with an alif in place of the hamza, Ibn Dhakwan with a quiescent hamza, and Hamzah, when pausing, pronounces it between between. ﴿So when he fell, the jinn realized﴾, i.e., the jinn knew after the matter had been confused for them.

﴿Had the jinn known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾: that is, had they known the unseen as they claim, they would have known of his death the moment it occurred, and they would not have remained a year in subjection to him until he fell. So he wished to conceal his death from them so that they would complete it, and he summoned them, and they built over him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and his soul was taken while he leaned upon it. He remained so until the termite ate the staff and he fell. Then they opened [the palace] for him, and they wished to know the time of his death, so they placed the termite on the staff, and it ate for a day and a night, a quantity. They calculated from that and found that he had died a year earlier. His lifespan was fifty-three years, and he ruled from the age of thirteen, and he began the building of Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign.

﴿Indeed there was for Saba'﴾, i.e., for the descendants of Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr denied it the nunation (sarf), because it became the name of a tribe. From Ibn Kathir is also reported the changing of its hamza to an alif, perhaps he pronounced it between between, and the narrator did not convey it as it should have been. (﴿in their dwellings﴾) in their places of residence. These are in Yemen, called Ma'rib, between it and San'a' is a three-day journey. Hamzah and Hafs read it in the singular with a fatha, and al-Kisa'i with a kasra, treating it as an irregular form, like al-masjid and al-matla'. ﴿A sign﴾, an indicator pointing to the existence of the Creator who chooses, and that He is capable of whatever He wills of wondrous matters, a metaphor for the good and the wicked, supporting the preceding proof, as in the stories of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both. ﴿Two gardens﴾ is a substitute for "a sign," or a deleted predicate, its estimate being: the sign is two gardens. It is also read in the accusative as a praise. The meaning is two groups of orchards.

﴿On the right and on the left﴾: one group on the right of their town and another group on its left, each of them, in their closeness and compactness, as if they were a single garden; or, two gardens, each man's garden to the right of his dwelling and to its left. ﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾: a report of what their prophet said to them, or the language of the situation, or an indication that they were deserving of being told this. ﴿A good land and a forgiving Lord﴾: a resumed statement to indicate what necessitates gratitude, i.e., this town in which your provision is, is a good town, and your Lord who provided for you and sought your gratitude is a forgiving Lord who overlooks the shortcomings of whoever thanks Him. It is also read as "al-kull" in the accusative as a praise. It is said that it was the most fertile and the best of lands, having no blight nor harmful creature in it.

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil* (Commentary on Surah 34, verses 18–19):

﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed⦆ by extending provision to their people, and these are the towns of al-Sham (Greater Syria). ﴿Towns visible⦆ connected to one another, so that some of them are visible from others; or [they were] situated along the main road, visible to travellers. ﴿And We made the travel in them measured⦆ such that the one who sets out in the morning rests in one town and the one who sets out in the afternoon spends the night in another, until he reaches al-Sham. ﴿Travel in them⦆ as if it were said by the tongue of the state or by the tongue of speech. ﴿Nights and days⦆ whenever you wish, of night or of day. ﴿Secure⦆ the security there does not vary with the variation of times; or, travel in them secure, even if your journey there lasts long; or, travel in them for the nights and days of your lives, you will meet in them only security.

﴿They said: Our Lord, make the distances of our journeys far⦆. They became ungrateful for the blessing and grew weary of well-being, like the Children of Israel, so they asked God to place between them and al-Sham deserts, so that they could display their superiority over the poor by riding mounts and taking provisions. So God answered them by ruining the intervening towns.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read «بَعِّدْ» (*ba'\u0302\u0313\u0331'\u0331ID*, with the verb in the imperative and a shadda on the ʿayn). Ya'qub read ﴿Our Lord, make far⦆ in the form of a report, as a complaint from them about the length of their journey, out of excess in luxury and failure to acknowledge the blessings God had bestowed upon them. Similar is the reading of one who read «رَبَّنا بَعِّدْ» or «بَعُدَ», as a vocative address with the verb ascribed to *bayna* (between).

﴿And they wronged themselves⦆ in that they were insolent toward the blessing and did not acknowledge it. ﴿So We made them into tales⦆ which people speak of with wonder, and it became a proverb; they say: "They were scattered like the hands of Saba'." ﴿And We tore them completely apart⦆ by dispersing them to the utmost degree, so that Ghassan among them went to al-Sham, Anmar to Yathrib, Judham to Tihamah, and the Azd to Oman. ﴿Indeed in that⦆ in what has been mentioned, ﴿are signs for every steadfast one⦆ against sins, ﴿grateful⦆ for blessings.

And Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them, and they followed him, except for a group of the believers. (Qur'an 34:20)

That is, he was truthful in his assumption, or he was truthful with regard to his assumption, the verb being used like *faʿalta juhdaka* ("you did your utmost"). The verb may also take its object directly, as in *ṣadaqa waʿdahu* ("he fulfilled his promise"), since it is a kind of speech. The Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa) read it with the doubled letter, meaning "he made his assumption come true" or "he found it true." It is also read with *Iblīs* in the accusative and *al-ẓann* in the nominative, with the doubling, meaning "his assumption found him truthful." With the single letter, it means "his assumption told him the truth when it imagined to him their seduction." It is also read with both the nominative and the single letter, *ʿalā al-abdān* ("on the [reading of] al-abdān" as printed), and this may refer to his assumption about Sheba when he saw them immersed in desires, or about the children of Adam when he saw that their father, the Prophet (ﷺ), had weak resolve, or to the desire and anger that were composed within them, or to what he heard from the angels when they said: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ (2:30), whereupon he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them﴾ and ﴿I will surely misguide them﴾ (4:119).

﴿...except a group of the believers﴾: "except a group" who are the believers and did not follow him. Their small number is relative to the disbelievers. Or it means "except a group from among the groups of the believers who did not follow him in disobedience," and these are the sincere ones.

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾: no domination or power through whispering and seduction.

﴿...except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from one who is in doubt about it﴾: except so that Our knowledge would be attached to that in a way that results in reward, or so that the believer is distinguished from the doubter, or so that the one whose faith was predestined would believe and the one whose misguidance was predestined would doubt. The meaning of attaining knowledge here is the attainment of its object, for emphasis. In the construction of the two relative clauses there is a subtle point that is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 22–23:

﴿Say﴾ to the polytheists. ﴿Call upon those whom you claimed﴾, i.e., whom you claimed to be gods. Here, the two objects of zaʿama (to claim, to assert) are involved: the first has been omitted because of the length of the relative pronoun with its complement (ṭūl al-mawṣūl bi-ṣilatih), and the second because its descriptive phrase stands in its place. It is not permissible for the second object to be the pronoun (hu), because the sentence would not hold together with the pronoun, nor with ﴿they possess not﴾, because they do not claim it. ﴿Besides Allah﴾. The meaning is: call upon them concerning what concerns you of bringing about a benefit or repelling a harm, so that perhaps they will respond to you, if your claim is valid. Then He answered on their behalf, indicating that the answer is determined and that it does not admit of obstinacy, and said: ﴿They possess not an atom's weight﴾ of good or evil. ﴿In the heavens nor in the earth﴾, in any matter. He mentioned both for general customary inclusiveness (al-ʿumūm al-ʿurfī), or because some of their gods are heavenly, such as the angels and the stars, and some are earthly, such as the idols, or because the proximate causes of harm and good are both heavenly and earthly. The sentence is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) to clarify their condition. ﴿And they have no share therein﴾, no partnership (shirka), neither in creation nor in ownership. ﴿And He has not among them any supporter﴾ who helps Him in managing their affairs.

﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him﴾, so intercession will not benefit them either, as they claim, since intercession does not benefit with Allah. ﴿Except for one whom He permits﴾: He permits him to intercede, or He permits that intercession be made on his behalf, due to the elevation of his station, though this has not been established. The lam is, according to the first reading, like the lam in your saying: "The generosity is for Zayd," and according to the second, like the lam in your saying: "I came to you for Zayd." It is not permissible for the second object to be the pronoun (hu), because the sentence would not hold together with the pronoun, nor with ﴿they possess not﴾, because they do not claim it. ﴿Besides Allah﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 24:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?"﴾ He intends by this the affirmation of His statement ﴿They do not possess﴾. ﴿Say: "Allah."﴾ For there is no answer other than this. It also indicates that if they remain silent or hesitate in answering, out of fear of being pressed, they nevertheless acknowledge it in their hearts. ﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ That is: indeed one of the two groups, the monotheists, who are singled out for provision and for independent power and worship, or the polytheists, who associate with Him lifeless matter descended to the lowest degree of contingent existence, is surely upon one of the two clear matters, guidance or error. And this, after the eloquent affirmation that has preceded, which points to who is upon guidance and who is in error, is more forceful than explicit declaration, because it takes the form of fairness, which silences the contentious opponent. Its parallel is the saying of Hassan:

Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal? Then the evil of you both is a ransom for the good of you both.

It has been said that it is an instance of al-laff wa-l-nashr (intertwining and unfolding), but this is open to scrutiny. The difference between the two particles [is because] the guide is like one who has climbed a minaret, looking at things and surveying them, or one who has mounted a steed and drives it wherever he wishes; while the one who is astray is as if he is immersed in confused darkness, seeing nothing, or imprisoned in a pit from which he cannot escape.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 25–26:

﴿Say: You will not be questioned about what we committed in sin, nor will we be questioned about what you do.﴾ This is more equitable and more eloquent in humility, since the sin is attributed to themselves (ʾanfusihim) and the action to the addressees.

﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Then He will judge between us with truth﴾ He will decide and separate, by admitting the people of truth to the Garden and the people of falsehood to the Fire. ﴿And He is the Opener﴾ the Judge who decides matters that are closed (al-munghalaqa). ﴿The All-Knowing﴾ of what ought to be decided by it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 27–28:

﴿Say: "Show me those whom you have joined with Him as partners."﴾ (He says:) "Show me by what attribute you have joined them with God in the entitlement to worship." This is an inquiry into their doubt after the proof has been established against them, as an added rebuke to them. ﴿Nay!﴾ is a reprimand to them against associating partners, after the refutation of the comparison.

﴿Rather, He is God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, the One described with dominance, perfect power and wisdom. And those who are joined with Him are characterized by abasement, refusing outright to accept knowledge and power. The pronoun refers either to God or to the matter (al-sha'n, the affair/subject).

﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive (kaffatan) messenger to mankind﴾: except as a general mission to them, from kaff (restraint), for when it encompasses them, it restrains (kaffat) any of them from leaving it. Or: except as one who gathers them together in the conveying (of the message). In this case it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the kaf and the ta' (the pronoun suffix of the verb and the feminine marker), for emphasis. It is not permissible, according to the preferred view, to make it a circumstantial clause from "mankind" (al-nas). ﴿Bearer of good news and warner, but most of mankind do not know﴾, so their ignorance drives them to oppose you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 29–30:

[The disbelievers say] "When is this promise?" out of the extremity of their ignorance. "This promise" means that which is given as glad tidings and warned of, or the promised event mentioned in His saying: ﴿Our Lord will gather us together﴾. "If you are truthful" — they address this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers.

﴿Say: For you is the appointment of a Day﴾: a promised day, or the time of a promise. Its annexation to "day" (yawm) is for specification (al-tabyin). What supports this is that it was read as "yawmi" (in the genitive, as a substitution, badal), and it was read as "yawman" with an implied verb, meaning "I mean a day." ﴿You cannot delay from it an hour, nor advance [it]﴾ when it comes upon you. This is a reply of threat, coming in correspondence with what they intended by their question of obstinacy and denial.(p-248)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 31–32:

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in that which came before it."﴾ Nor in the books that came before it which indicate the description (na't) of the Prophet. It is said that the disbelievers of Makkah asked the People of the Book about the Messenger (ﷺ), and they informed them that they find his description in their books. So they became angry and said that. It is also said that "that which came before it" refers to the Day of Resurrection. ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord﴾, that is, at the place of reckoning. ﴿Blaming one another, saying﴾ they argue with each other and throw words back and forth. ﴿Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant﴾, that is, the followers say to the leaders, ﴿"Had it not been for you, we would have been believers"﴾, had it not been for your misguiding us and your barring us from faith. ﴿"We would have been believers"﴾ by following the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed, "Did we avert you from guidance after it came to you? Rather, you were criminals."﴾ They denied that they had been barring them from faith, and affirmed that it was they themselves who had barred their own souls, in that they turned away from guidance and preferred imitation (taqlid) over it. For this reason they framed the denial in the form of a question (istifham).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 33:

﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant: "Nay, it was your scheming by night and day, when you commanded us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him."﴾ (The word "bal", "nay", is) a turning away from their (the arrogant's) own statement. That is: our sins did not prevent (you from faith); rather, your scheming against us was ceaseless, night and day, until you led our opinion astray. ﴿When you commanded us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him﴾. The conjunction (al-'atif, "when") attaches it to their first statement. The construction of "makr" (scheming) with the time-expression is an extension of usage (ittisa'). It has also been read as "makra al-layli" with the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), as "makrun al-layla" with tanwin and the accusative of the time-expression, and as "makarru al-layli" from al-kurur (recurrence).

﴿And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment﴾. Both groups harboured regret over misguidance and misguiding others, and each concealed it from his companion for fear of reproach. Alternatively, they displayed it, for (the verb) is among the words with opposite meanings (addad), since the hamza (in "asarru") can signify either affirmation or negation, as in "ashkaytuhu" (I complained of him / I removed his complaint).

﴿And We will place the shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾. That is, upon their necks. He used the explicit noun (alladhina kafaru, "those who disbelieved") instead of a pronoun to express condemnation of them and to indicate the cause that warrants their shackles.

﴿Are they being recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ That is, nothing is done to them except as a recompense for their deeds. The transitive construction of "yujza" is either by including the sense of "yaqdi" (to decree/requite) or by omitting the preposition.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 34–36:

﴿Never did We send a warner to any town but its affluent ones said: "We disbelieve in what you have been sent with."﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from his people. The singling out of the affluent for denial is because the motive that most drives one to it is arrogance and boasting in the adornments of this world, immersion in desires, and contempt for those who have not been granted a share of them. For this reason they combined mockery and boasting with denial, saying: ﴿We disbelieve in what you have been sent with﴾, in correspondence of plural to plural.

﴿And they said: "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ Meaning: we are therefore more deserving of what you claim, if it is possible. ﴿And we will not be punished﴾ either because punishment will not befall us, or because He has honored us with this, so He will not humiliate us with punishment.

﴿Say﴾ in refutation of their assumption: ﴿Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾. For this reason individuals who are alike in their qualities and attributes differ in it. Had it been due to honor or humiliation that necessitates it, it would not have been by His will. ﴿But most people do not know﴾, so they suppose that abundance of wealth and children is for nobility and honor, whereas it often is for gradual enticement (istidraj), as He said:

Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in closeness (**qurbah**, nearness). The relative pronoun **allati** (feminine) is used either because the intended meaning is "the group of your wealth and your children," or because it is an attribute of an omitted noun such as **al-taqwa** (piety) or **al-khaslah** (quality). It was also read as **bi-alladhi** (masculine), meaning "by the thing which brings you near."

﴿Except for one who believes and does righteous deeds﴾ is an exception (**istithna'**) from the object of **tuqarribukum** (brings you near). That is: wealth and children bring no one near except the believing righteous person who spends his wealth in the way of God, teaches his child good, and raises him upon righteousness. Alternatively, it is an exception from "your wealth and your children," with an omitted modifier (**mudaf**) understood.

﴿Then those, for them is the recompense of double﴾: they will be repaid with double, up to ten times and more. The construction is an idafah (genitive construction) of the verbal noun (**masdar**) to its object. It was read as **bil-a'mal** (with the deeds) according to the original form. It is also reported from Ya'qub that both words were read in the nominative (**raf'**), as a substitution (**badal**) for "double." The word **jaza'** (recompense) is in the accusative as a specification (**tamyiz**) or as a verbal noun (**masdar**) for a verb implied by **lahum** (for them).

﴿For what they did, and they are in the lofty chambers, secure﴾ from hardships. It was read with a fatha and with a sukun on the **ra'** (**al-ghurafat** and **al-ghurfat**). Hamzah read **fi al-ghurfah** (in the chamber), in the sense of the genus.

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by rejecting and disparaging them, ﴿seeking to frustrate [them]﴾: racing against Our prophets, or thinking that they can escape Us.

﴿Those, in the punishment they will be brought forth.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verses 40–41:

(And on the Day when We gather them all together) the arrogant and the oppressed, (then We will say to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?") — a rebuke to the polytheists, a reproach to them, and a dashing of their hopes of the intercession they expected from [their deities]. The singling out of the angels is because they are the most noble of their associates and the ones fit for address among them, and because their worship is the origin and root of polytheism. Hafs and Ya'qub read the verb with the ya' (yaʾ, "they will say") in both places.

﴿They will say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them.﴾ You are the One whom we take as our ally, rather than them; there is no alliance between us and them." It is as if they thereby declared their disavowal of being content with their worship. Then they turned away from that and denied that they had truly worshipped them, by their saying: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, that is, the devils, inasmuch as they obeyed them in worshipping other than God. It was also said: they would appear to them in forms and make them imagine that they were the angels, so they worshipped them. ﴿Most of them were believers in them﴾. The first pronoun refers to humankind or to the polytheists, and "most" is used in the sense of "all"; the second pronoun refers to the jinn.

﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm another﴾, since the command in that Day is entirely His, because the abode is the abode of recompense, and He alone is the Recompenser. ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong: "Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny."﴾ It is conjoined (ʿatf) to (lā yamlik, "will not have power"), explaining the purpose intended by its preface.

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, they say: "This is nothing but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship."﴾ They mean Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. ﴿And they say: "This is nothing but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship"﴾, so he drags you into following what he has innovated. ﴿And they say: "This is nothing"﴾, meaning the Qur'an. ﴿but a fabrication (ifk)﴾, because what is in it does not correspond to reality, ﴿invented (muftara)﴾ by attributing it to God, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿And those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them﴾, referring to the matter of prophethood, or to Islam, or to the Qur'an; the first is in terms of its meaning, and this is in terms of its wording and its inimitability. ﴿"This is nothing but clear sorcery."﴾ Its being sorcery is evident. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 46:

﴿Say: I admonish you with one thing﴾ I guide you and give you sincere advice with one trait, which is what the following indicates: ﴿that you stand up for Allah﴾, namely, standing up from the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or taking a stand in the matter sincerely for the sake of Allah, turning away from disputation (mira') and blind imitation (taqlid). ﴿Two by two and one by one﴾, dispersed, two by two and one by one, for crowding disturbs the mind and confuses speech. ﴿Then you reflect⁠﴾ upon the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he has brought, so that you may know its reality. Its grammatical position is in the genitive as a substitute (badal) or an explanation (bayan), or in the nominative or accusative by an implied "he" (huwa) or "I mean" (a'ni). ﴿There is no madness in your companion﴾, so that you may know what madness in him would drive him to this. Or it is a resumed statement (isti'naf) alerting them that the soundness of intellect they knew him to have is sufficient to establish the weight of his truthfulness, for he would not allow himself to undertake a matter of great gravity and a grave affair without certainty and reliance on proof, so that he would be disgraced before the eyes of witnesses and cast himself into destruction. How much more so, since many miracles have been joined to him. It has been said that "ma" is interrogative, and the meaning is: then you reflect what kind of trace of madness is in him. ﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾, before him, because he has been sent at the approach of the Hour (nasam al-sa'ah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say: Whatever reward I have asked of you﴾ — i.e., whatever reward I have asked of you for the message. ﴿then it is yours﴾ — the intended meaning is the negation of asking for it. It is as if he made the claim of prophethood entail one of two matters: either madness, or the expectation of some worldly benefit from it, because he (the claimant) either does it for a purpose or not for a purpose, and whichever it is, one of the two follows. Then he negated each of them. It has also been said that (mā) is a relative pronoun, meaning what he asked them with His words: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it, except that whoever wills may take a way to his Lord﴾ [25:57], and His words: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the kinship﴾ [42:23]. Taking the way benefits them, and "its kinship" (qurbāhu) is their kinship. ﴿My reward is only from Allah, and He is over all things a witness﴾ — an observer who knows my truthfulness and the sincerity of my intention. Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (the yā' of ajriya) with a sukun (silent yā').

﴿Say: "Indeed, my Lord hurls down the truth."﴾ He casts it and sends it down upon whomever He chooses from among His servants. Or He hurls the truth against falsehood, so that it crushes it. It was also read in the accusative as an attribute of (rabbi), or as implied by (a'ni, "I mean"). It was said that "the falsehood" refers to Iblis or to the idol; the meaning is that it creates no creation and does not bring it back, or that it originates no good for its people and does not restore it.

It was also said that (ma) is interrogative, governing what follows it.

Say: "If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment. But if I am rightly guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near."

The verse's wording, "if I go astray" (in ﴿ضَلَلْتُ﴾), refers to straying from the truth. "Then I only go astray to my own detriment" (﴿فَإنَّما أضِلُّ عَلى نَفْسِي﴾): the harm of my straying falls upon me, because it is through me, since the soul is the one that is ignorant of its essence (al-Jahila bil-Dhat) and the one that commands to evil (al-Ammara bil-Su'). On this basis, he matched the conditional clause with his words, "And if I am rightly guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me" (﴿وَإنِ اهْتَدَيْتُ فَبِما يُوحِي إلَيَّ رَبِّي﴾), for the guidance is by His guidance and His grant of success (tawfiq). "Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Ever-Near" (﴿إنَّهُ سَمِيعٌ قَرِيبٌ﴾): He perceives the speech of every one who goes astray and of every one who is rightly guided, and their deeds, even if they conceal them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 34, verse 51:

﴿And if you could see when they are terrified﴾ at death, or at the Resurrection, or on the Day of Badr. The response of (law, "if") is omitted; its implied sense is: "you would see a dreadful matter." ﴿Then there is no escape﴾: they will not escape Allah by flight or by seeking refuge in a fortress. ﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾: from the surface of the earth to its depths; or from the place of standing (on the Day of Resurrection) to the Fire; or from the desert of Badr to the well (al-qalib). The conjunction is with (fazi'u, "they were terrified"), or with (la fawt, "there is no escape"). It is supported by the fact that it has been read as (wa-ukhidha, "and he was seized"), in coordination with its place (mahall), meaning: "there is no escape there, and there he was seized."
